Style rule explanation:
log in & log out (verbs)
Databricks style is: Use "log in" or "log out" to refer to logging in or out of Databricks. This goes against the current industry standard terminology for cloud-based services. The industry standard is "sign in " or "sign out" (AWS, Microsoft, and Google). Use "log in to," not "log into." Don't use "log on" or "log off."

sign in & sign out (verbs)
It's OK if you use "sign in" or "sign out" to refer to signing in or out of a cloud provider or other software because that's the industry standard terminology.

login, logout, logon (noun or adjective)
Avoid using "login" or "logout" as a noun or adjective. Use the label of the dialog or window that you're talking about logging in or out of instead. Do not hyphenate "login" or "logout" when you use them as nouns or adjectives. Don't use "logon."

sign-in, sign-out (noun or adjective)
Avoid using "sign-in" or "sign-out" as a noun or adjective. Use the label of the dialog or window that you're talking about signing in to or out of instead. Always hyphenate "sign-in" or "sign-out" and include the noun your modifying when you use them as nouns or adjectives (for example, "sign-in dialog" or "sign-out page"). Don't use "signin", "sign on", or "signon."
Examples:
Correct:
Log in to your Databricks account.
Log out of your Databricks account.
Sign in to your AWS account.
Sign out of your AWS account.
In the "Sign in to your account" dialog, type your admin account password.

Avoid, but OK:
In the login dialog, type your admin account password.
On the sign-in page, type your admin account password.

Incorrect:
Log-in to your Databricks account.
Log into your Databricks account.
Logout of your Databricks account.
Sign-in to your AWS account.
Close the signout dialog.

Rules for "which":

- If you can omit the clause and the sentence still makes sense, use "which".
- Put a comma before "which".
